beats.intro: Lesson twenty-three. [[sub]]Why no management style is best, and the one variable that decides which style works.
beats.nobest: Is there one best way to manage? [[fashion]]Over the years, the favoured style followed the theory of motivation of the day. [[y1900]]Around nineteen hundred, people were told what to do. Do it and be paid; don't, and be fired. Orders went down and were carried out without question. [[fifties]]In the nineteen-fifties, a humanistic view took over: there was a nicer way to get people to work. [[lab]]Then behavioural scientists put the theories to careful tests. [[none]]Surprisingly, no style came out better than the others. [[rule]]There seems to be no single best style.
beats.rotate: Grove saw the same thing at Intel. [[rot]]Middle managers were often rotated between similar groups, to broaden their experience. Some pairings produced far more than others. [[swap]]But when the managers were switched around, [[after]]neither the managers nor the groups kept their high or low output. [[pair]]High output came from particular managers with particular groups. [[style]]So a given approach does not work equally well everywhere.
beats.trm: Some researchers say one variable tells you the best style: [[trm]]the task-relevant maturity of the people you supervise. TRM, for short. [[mix]]It combines their drive to achieve and their readiness to take responsibility, [[edu]]with their education, training and experience. [[task]]And it is specific to the task at hand. [[two]]The same person can be high in one job and low in another. [[back]]You met it in lessons six and eight, setting how often to check and to meet. Here is the full idea.
beats.q1: Quick check. High or low, for this task?
beats.sales: Grove's example. [[star]]Intel moved a very productive sales manager from the field to run a factory unit, a job of similar size. [[drop]]His performance fell, and he showed the signs of someone overwhelmed. [[why]]His personal maturity had not changed. But the environment, the content and the tasks were all new, so his TRM was very low. [[grow]]In time he learned, his TRM rose, and his performance climbed back toward its old level. [[conf]]It should have been predictable. Intel had confused general competence with task-relevant maturity.
beats.freeway: TRM can also drop when the job changes around you. [[pace]]Someone may handle a certain level of complexity and uncertainty well. Then the pace speeds up, or the job abruptly changes. [[road]]Think of someone with years of driving on quiet country roads, [[fwy]]suddenly put on a crowded city freeway. [[drop]]Same car, same driver. Their TRM drops sharply.
beats.styles: So different levels of TRM call for different styles. [[axis]]Grove's table sets them out. [[low]]When TRM is low, be structured and task-oriented. Tell them what to do, when, and how. [[med]]As it grows, shift to a style centred on the individual: two-way communication, support, and reasoning things through together. Your attention moves from the task to the person. [[high]]When TRM is high, keep your involvement minimal: agree on the objectives, then monitor. [[first]]Judge the maturity first. The style follows.
beats.monitor: One thing never changes. [[band]]At every level of TRM, monitor closely enough to avoid surprises. [[del]]As lesson six said, monitoring is the difference between delegating a task, [[abd]]and abdicating it.
beats.nice: A warning. [[nice]]Don't judge styles as nice or not nice. [[worthy]]A structured style is not less worthy than a communicating one. [[eff]]The only question is whether it is effective.
beats.parent: Grove compares all this to raising a child, [[age]]where the right style changes with the child's age. [[tod]]A toddler can't understand that a vase is a priceless heirloom, but he can understand no. [[bike]]Later comes the first two-wheeler. The parent doesn't send him off alone, but runs alongside, steadying the bike and talking about safety. [[alone]]Later still, he rides off without the litany of rules. [[coll]]Finally he leaves for college, and the parent just monitors his progress. [[back]]But if he runs into severe trouble at school, the parent may go back to an earlier style.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]No single management style is best. [[w2]]The variable that decides is task-relevant maturity, and it is specific to each task. [[w3]]Low TRM: tell what, when and how. Medium: talk it through. High: agree on objectives and monitor. [[w4]]Always monitor enough to avoid surprises. [[w5]]Judge a style by whether it works, and move back when TRM drops. Now the lesson practice.
